column9: stem
column14: option_a
column15: option_b
column16: option_c
column17: option_d
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: What is the main thing that decides whether a form of cellular transport is active or passive?
column14: Whether the cell has to spend energy (ATP) to move the material
column15: How big the cell is
column16: Whether it happens in a plant cell, which has a wall, or an animal cell
column17: Whether the material being moved is water
column28: Active transport uses the cell's energy (ATP); passive transport does not. Cell size, cell type, and whether the material is water do not decide it. A common mistake is thinking anything involving water is passive and everything else is active.
column29: Think about what the word active means for you: doing work.

column9: The energy molecule that a cell spends to run active transport is ___.
column28: Cells spend ATP (adenosine triphosphate) to power pumps and to move vesicles. A common mistake is answering glucose; glucose is food that gets turned into ATP, but the pump itself runs on ATP.
column29: It is a three-letter abbreviation.

column9: What is a concentration gradient?
column14: A protein that pumps ions across the cell membrane using ATP
column15: A membrane that lets only water through
column16: The moment a cell bursts from taking in too much water
column17: A difference in how much of a substance is in two areas
column28: A concentration gradient is a difference in concentration between two areas, like lots of a substance inside a cell and little outside. Particles move down the gradient on their own. Students sometimes confuse the gradient with the pump that works against it.
column29: Gradient is like a slope: one side is high and the other is low.

column9: A tea bag is dropped into a mug of hot water. Without stirring, the brown color spreads out from the bag into the rest of the water. Overall, which way are the tea particles moving?
column14: From the bag (high concentration) out into the water (low concentration)
column15: From the water (low concentration) into the bag (high concentration)
column16: Only straight down to the bottom of the mug
column17: They are not moving; the water is changing color on its own as it slowly cools
column28: This is diffusion: tea particles spread from where they are crowded (in and near the bag) to where there are few (the rest of the water). A common mistake is thinking particles crowd together; on their own they always spread out.
column29: Where is the color darkest at the start?

column9: A coffee filter lets liquid coffee drip through but holds back the coffee grounds. This is a good model for which property of the cell membrane?
column14: Active transport
column15: Equilibrium
column16: Exocytosis
column17: Selective permeability
column28: The filter lets some things through and blocks others, just like a selectively permeable membrane. Equilibrium is an even spread, active transport uses energy, and exocytosis uses vesicles. Students sometimes pick equilibrium because the coffee ends up evenly mixed, but the filter's job is choosing what passes.
column29: The filter is picky about what it lets through. Which word means picky?

column9: The cell membrane is made mostly of a double layer of which molecules?
column14: Phospholipids
column15: Starch
column16: Cellulose
column17: DNA
column28: The membrane is a phospholipid bilayer: two layers of phospholipids with proteins set into it. Cellulose makes plant cell walls, not membranes, which is a common mix-up.
column29: Bi- means two, and the membrane is called a ___ bilayer.

column9: A shriveled raisin soaks in a bowl of water overnight and becomes plump. Water moved into the raisin's cells by ___.
column28: The movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane is osmosis. The raisin's cells have more sugar (solute) than the bowl of water, so water moves in. A common mistake is answering diffusion; osmosis is the special name for water diffusing across a membrane.
column29: Which form of transport is only about water crossing a membrane?

column9: Which form of transport moves molecules through a channel or carrier protein from high to low concentration without using ATP?
column14: Simple diffusion
column15: Active transport
column16: Facilitated diffusion
column17: Exocytosis
column28: Facilitated diffusion is passive (no ATP, high to low) but uses a protein to help. Simple diffusion uses no protein, and active transport uses ATP. Students often pick active transport just because a protein is involved.
column29: Facilitate means to help. Which choice has a helper but no energy cost?

column9: Match each word part to its meaning.
column14: Hypo- :: Under or less
column15: Hyper- :: Over or more
column16: Iso- :: Equal or the same
column17: Endo- :: Into or inside
column28: Hypo- means under (a hypotonic solution has less solute), hyper- means over (more solute), iso- means equal, endo- means into, and exo- means out. Students often flip hypo- and hyper-; think of a hypodermic needle going under the skin.
column29: A hyperactive kid has more energy than normal. Start there.

column9: Cells lining your small intestine keep absorbing glucose from your food even after there is more glucose inside the cells than in the intestine. Which form of transport must they be using?
column14: Simple diffusion
column15: Osmosis
column16: Facilitated diffusion
column17: Active transport
column28: Once there is more glucose inside, moving even more in is going from low to high concentration, against the gradient. That takes energy, so it is active transport. Facilitated diffusion uses a protein too, but it can only move glucose from high to low.
column29: Which way is the glucose moving compared with its gradient?

column9: A white blood cell wraps its membrane around a bacterium and pulls it inside in a sac. Which form of transport is this?
column14: Endocytosis
column15: Exocytosis
column16: Osmosis
column17: Facilitated diffusion
column28: Taking a large particle into the cell by folding the membrane around it is endocytosis (this "cell eating" is also called phagocytosis). Exocytosis is the reverse, sending material out. A bacterium is far too big for a channel protein.
column29: Endo- means into and exo- means out of. Which way is the bacterium going?

column9: Cells in your salivary glands pack digestive enzymes into sacs. The sacs fuse with the cell membrane and dump the enzymes outside the cell. Which form of transport is this?
column14: Endocytosis
column15: Simple diffusion
column16: Exocytosis
column17: Active transport by a pump
column28: A vesicle fusing with the membrane to release its contents outside is exocytosis. Endocytosis brings material in. A pump moves single ions or molecules, not sacs of enzymes. Students often mix up endo- and exo-; exo- means exit.
column29: Are the enzymes going into the cell or out of it?

column9: A sugar cube dissolves in a cup of tea. After a long time, the sugar is spread evenly through the whole cup with no gradient left. The sugar has reached ___.
column28: When a substance is evenly spread and there is no concentration gradient, it has reached equilibrium. The molecules keep moving, but there is no net change. A common mistake is thinking the molecules stop moving at equilibrium.
column29: The word starts with equi-, meaning equal.

column9: The inside of a cell is 1% salt. Which solution is hypertonic to this cell?
column14: 0% salt (distilled water)
column15: 0.5% salt
column16: 1% salt
column17: 5% salt
column28: Hypertonic means the solution has MORE solute than the cell. Only 5% is higher than 1%. 1% would be isotonic, and 0% and 0.5% are hypotonic. Students often flip hypo- and hyper-.
column29: Hyper- means over. Which solution has more salt than the cell?

column9: A cell that is 2% sugar inside sits in a beaker of 2% sugar solution. The solution is ___ to the cell.
column28: When the solute concentration is the same inside and outside, the solution is isotonic (iso- means equal). Water still crosses both ways, but there is no net change in the cell's size.
column29: Iso- means equal.

column9: Water will move INTO a cell by osmosis when the cell is placed in which kind of solution?
column14: Hypertonic
column15: Isotonic
column16: Any solution, because water always enters cells
column17: Hypotonic
column28: A hypotonic solution has less solute (more water) than the cell, so water moves into the cell. In a hypertonic solution water leaves; in an isotonic one there is no net movement. A common mistake is choosing hypertonic because hyper sounds like more water, but the prefix describes the solute.
column29: The prefix describes the amount of solute outside. Water moves toward more solute.

column9: A limp, wilted stalk of celery is left standing in a glass of plain tap water overnight. In the morning it is firm and crisp again. What happened?
column14: Water moved into the celery cells by osmosis and pushed against the cell walls
column15: Salt moved out of the celery by active transport, making the cells firm
column16: The celery made new cell walls overnight
column17: Water left the celery cells overnight, which made the whole stalk harder and stiffer
column28: Tap water is hypotonic to celery cells, so water moves in by osmosis. The swollen cells press against their stiff cell walls (turgor pressure), and the stalk becomes firm. A common mistake is thinking crisp means the cells lost water.
column29: Which has more dissolved stuff: tap water or the inside of a celery cell?

column9: Which of these needs help from a membrane protein to cross the phospholipid bilayer?
column14: An oxygen molecule (O₂)
column15: A carbon dioxide molecule (CO₂)
column16: A potassium ion (K⁺)
column17: None of them; all three slip straight through
column28: Ions like K⁺ carry an electric charge, so the oily middle of the bilayer blocks them; they need a channel or pump. O₂ and CO₂ are small and uncharged, so they slip right between the phospholipids. Students often think size is the only thing that matters, but charge matters too.
column29: Look for the one with a + sign. Charged particles do not mix with the oily tails.

column9: Endocytosis and exocytosis are both forms of active transport, because the cell spends energy to move vesicles and reshape its membrane.
column28: True. Moving vesicles and folding or fusing the membrane takes energy (ATP), so bulk transport is classified as active. A common mistake is thinking only protein pumps count as active transport.
column29: Does building and moving a sac take work?

column9: Select every example of PASSIVE transport. Select all that apply.
column14: Oxygen moving from your blood into a muscle cell
column15: Water moving from damp soil into a root hair cell
column16: A white blood cell engulfing a yeast cell
column17: Glucose moving down its gradient through a carrier protein
column18: A nerve cell pumping sodium ions out using ATP
column19: A pancreas cell releasing insulin from vesicles
column28: Oxygen diffusing, water entering by osmosis, and glucose by facilitated diffusion all move high to low with no ATP, so they are passive. Engulfing (endocytosis), releasing from vesicles (exocytosis), and pumping with ATP are active. Students often leave out the glucose example because it uses a protein; a protein alone does not make it active.
column29: For each one ask: is the cell spending energy, or is the material just moving down its gradient?

column9: An amoeba takes in a smaller protist to eat it. Put the steps in order.
column14: The membrane pinches off, making a vesicle inside the amoeba
column15: The amoeba's cell membrane touches the protist
column16: The vesicle (food vacuole) holding the protist moves into the cytoplasm
column17: The membrane folds and wraps around the protist
column28: First the membrane contacts the protist, then folds around it, then pinches off into a vesicle, and finally the vesicle moves into the cytoplasm (where it can meet a lysosome to digest the food). This is endocytosis. A common mistake is putting the vesicle forming before the membrane wraps around.
column29: The amoeba has to reach its food before it can surround it.

column9: Which everyday object is the best model of a channel protein?
column14: A pump powered by a motor that pushes cars through
column15: A delivery truck that carries boxes in and out of a city
column16: A tunnel that only certain cars fit through
column17: A locked safe
column28: A channel protein is an opening through the membrane that lets specific particles pass down their gradient, like a tunnel that only fits certain cars. A motorized pump would model active transport, and a truck carrying boxes is more like a vesicle.
column29: A channel is an open path. Which choice is an open path?

column9: Pumping more air into a bike tire that is already full takes a lot of effort. Which form of cellular transport is most like this?
column14: Simple diffusion
column15: Osmosis
column16: Facilitated diffusion
column17: Active transport
column28: Pushing air into a tire that already has a lot of air is moving it from low to high pressure, against the gradient, which takes work. Active transport is the same: moving material from low to high concentration costs ATP. All the other choices are passive.
column29: Which form of transport costs the cell energy?

column9: During osmosis, water moves across a membrane toward the side that has
column14: more dissolved solute (and less water)
column15: less dissolved solute (and more water)
column16: a higher temperature
column17: no membrane at all
column28: Water moves from where there is more water (less solute) to where there is less water (more solute). A common mistake is thinking water moves toward more water; remember, water moves toward the salty or sugary side.
column29: Think about salt on a slug or a cucumber. Where does the water go?

column9: In ocean water, which is the solute and which is the solvent?
column14: Water is the solute; salt is the solvent
column15: Salt is the solute; water is the solvent
column16: Both are solutes
column17: Both are solvents
column28: The solute is the substance that dissolves (salt); the solvent does the dissolving (water). Students often mix up the two words; the solvent is usually the one there is the most of.
column29: Which one does the dissolving?

column9: In bulk transport, large materials are carried into or out of the cell inside small membrane sacs called
column14: ribosomes
column15: chloroplasts
column16: vesicles
column17: cell walls
column28: Vesicles are small membrane sacs used in endocytosis and exocytosis. Ribosomes make proteins, chloroplasts do photosynthesis, and cell walls are outer support layers. None of those are sacs.
column29: Which choice is a small bubble made of membrane?

column9: Carbon dioxide leaving a working muscle cell is an example of exocytosis.
column28: False. CO₂ is a small molecule that simply diffuses out through the phospholipid bilayer from high concentration (inside) to low (outside). Exocytosis is for large materials packed in vesicles. A common mistake is calling anything that leaves the cell exocytosis.
column29: Is CO₂ big enough to need a vesicle?

column9: Moving molecules "uphill," from low concentration to high concentration, is called ___ transport.
column28: Moving against the concentration gradient takes energy, which is active transport. Passive transport only moves materials downhill, from high to low.
column29: Going uphill takes work.

column9: When a nerve cell fires, potassium ions flow out through open channel proteins, from high concentration inside to low concentration outside. Which form of transport is this?
column14: Active transport
column15: Endocytosis
column16: Simple diffusion
column17: Facilitated diffusion
column28: The ions move down their gradient (high to low) with no energy, but they need a protein channel, so it is facilitated diffusion. It is not simple diffusion because ions cannot cross the bilayer on their own. Students often say active transport just because a protein is involved.
column29: Check two things: which way is the gradient, and is a protein needed?

column9: Oxygen moves from the air sacs in your lungs, where there is a lot of it, into your blood, where there is less. Which form of transport is this?
column14: Simple diffusion
column15: Osmosis
column16: Active transport
column17: Exocytosis
column28: Oxygen is small and uncharged, and it moves high to low, so it diffuses right through the membranes. That is simple diffusion. Osmosis is only for water, and active transport moves things low to high.
column29: Oxygen is small and moving from a lot to a little.

column9: An animal cell is placed in a hypertonic solution. What will happen to the cell?
column14: It will swell and may burst
column15: It will stay exactly the same size
column16: It will shrink as water leaves
column17: It will grow a cell wall
column28: A hypertonic solution has more solute than the cell, so water leaves the cell by osmosis and the cell shrinks (shrivels). Swelling happens in a hypotonic solution. Students often mix these up because hyper sounds like it should make the cell bigger.
column29: Water moves toward the side with more solute. Which side is that?

column9: When a plant cell loses so much water that its cell membrane pulls away from the cell wall, the process is called
column14: photosynthesis
column15: exocytosis
column16: equilibrium
column17: plasmolysis
column28: Plasmolysis is when a plant cell loses water by osmosis and the membrane shrinks away from the stiff cell wall. It happens in a hypertonic solution, like salt water. The other terms describe different processes.
column29: The word comes from the plasma membrane pulling loose.

column9: Why does a plant cell in fresh water NOT burst the way an animal cell can?
column14: Its stiff cell wall pushes back and stops it from over-swelling
column15: Plant cells never take in water
column16: Its chloroplasts soak up the extra water
column17: Plant cells pump all the extra water back out of the cell using ATP
column28: Water does enter the plant cell, but the strong cell wall pushes back, so the cell gets firm instead of bursting. Animal cells have no cell wall, so they can swell until they burst. A common mistake is thinking water does not enter plant cells at all.
column29: What structure do plant cells have that animal cells do not?

column9: Which of these forms of transport uses ATP?
column14: Osmosis
column15: Facilitated diffusion (using a carrier protein)
column16: Phagocytosis (a cell engulfing a particle)
column17: Simple diffusion
column28: Phagocytosis is a kind of endocytosis, and moving the membrane around a particle takes energy. Osmosis, simple diffusion, and facilitated diffusion are all passive. Students sometimes choose facilitated diffusion because it uses a protein.
column29: Three of these are passive. Which one involves the cell doing work to swallow something?

column9: Which part of the cell membrane forms the channels and pumps that help materials cross?
column14: Phospholipid tails
column15: Starch molecules
column16: The cell wall
column17: Proteins
column28: Proteins set into the bilayer form channels, carriers, and pumps. The phospholipid tails make the oily middle that blocks many substances. The cell wall is outside the membrane and is not part of it.
column29: The membrane has two main building blocks: lipids and ___.

column9: Simple diffusion, osmosis, and facilitated diffusion all belong to the group called ___ transport.
column28: All three move materials down their concentration gradient without ATP, so they are passive transport. Active transport is the group that uses energy.
column29: There are two groups: active and ___.

column9: A salt solution is 15% salt. What percent of the solution is water?
column28: 100% − 15% salt = 85% water. In osmosis problems it helps to think about water: a solution with more solute has less water. A common mistake is answering 15 or adding to get 115.
column29: The salt and the water together make up 100%.

column9: In a lab, food coloring spreads 12 mm through a dish of gelatin in 4 minutes. What is the average rate of diffusion, in mm per minute?
column28: Rate = distance ÷ time = 12 mm ÷ 4 min = 3 mm per minute. A common mistake is multiplying (48) or dividing the wrong way (0.33).
column29: Rate means distance divided by time.

column9: A membrane protein that grabs a specific molecule, changes shape, and releases it on the other side is called a ___ protein.
column28: Carrier proteins bind a molecule and change shape to move it across. Channel proteins are open tunnels that do not need to change shape. Students often mix the two up.
column29: It carries the molecule across.

column9: Each phospholipid has a head that is attracted to water and two tails that avoid water. In the membrane, which part faces the watery inside and outside of the cell?
column14: The tails
column15: The heads
column16: Neither; the membrane has no water on either side
column17: Both the heads and the tails face the water equally
column28: The water-loving (hydrophilic) heads face the water on both sides, and the water-fearing (hydrophobic) tails hide in the middle. That oily middle is why charged particles and big molecules can't slip through on their own.
column29: Which part likes water?

column9: Which of these is an example of osmosis?
column14: Water moving from soil into a plant's root cells
column15: Carbon dioxide leaving a leaf
column16: Sugar dissolving in lemonade
column17: An amoeba surrounding a piece of food with its membrane
column28: Osmosis is water moving across a selectively permeable membrane, like water entering root cells. CO₂ leaving a leaf is simple diffusion, sugar dissolving is not membrane transport at all, and an amoeba surrounding food is endocytosis.
column29: Osmosis is always about one substance. Which choice is about it crossing a membrane?

column9: Why do particles spread out during diffusion, even with no stirring?
column14: The cell pushes them with ATP
column15: Gravity pulls them toward the side with fewer particles
column16: Particles are always moving and bumping randomly
column17: Particles are attracted to empty space and pulled into it
column28: Particles are in constant random motion. As they bump around, more of them end up moving from crowded areas into less crowded ones, so they spread out. No energy from the cell is needed, which is why diffusion is passive.
column29: Think about what particles are always doing, even in a still glass of water.

column9: Which of these can ONLY happen across a selectively permeable membrane?
column14: Food coloring spreading through a glass of water
column15: The smell of popcorn spreading through a room
column16: Sugar dissolving in hot tea
column17: Osmosis
column28: Osmosis is defined as water moving across a selectively permeable membrane. Food coloring and popcorn smell spread by diffusion, which can happen in open water or air with no membrane at all. Students often think all diffusion needs a membrane.
column29: Look for the process whose definition includes the word membrane.

column9: Match each form of transport to the best description.
column14: Simple diffusion :: Small molecules slip straight between the phospholipids
column15: Facilitated diffusion :: Molecules pass through a protein, no energy needed
column16: Active transport :: A protein pump uses ATP to move molecules against the gradient
column17: Exocytosis :: A vesicle fuses with the membrane and releases its contents outside
column28: Simple diffusion needs no help, facilitated diffusion uses a protein but no energy, active transport uses a pump and ATP, and exocytosis uses a vesicle. A common mistake is matching facilitated diffusion with the pump just because both use proteins.
column29: Sort by two questions: does it use a protein, and does it use energy?

column9: Plant cells have both a cell wall and a cell membrane. Which one is selectively permeable and controls what enters and leaves the cell?
column14: The cell wall
column15: The cell membrane
column16: Both control it equally
column17: Neither; the nucleus controls it
column28: The cell membrane is selectively permeable and decides what crosses. The cell wall is a stiff support layer that lets water and most dissolved materials pass right through. Students often assume the outermost layer is the gatekeeper.
column29: One of these is for support. The other is the gatekeeper.

column9: A gummy bear (made mostly of sugar and gelatin) is left in a cup of plain water overnight. In the morning it is much bigger. Which explanation is best?
column14: Water moved in because the gummy bear had more solute than the water
column15: Sugar moved into the gummy bear from the water
column16: The gummy bear used active transport to pump water in from the cup
column17: Water moved out of the gummy bear, and the leftover gelatin expanded as it dried
column28: The gummy bear is full of sugar, so the plain water is hypotonic to it. Water moves toward the higher solute concentration, into the gummy bear. A gummy bear is not alive, so it cannot use active transport; this shows osmosis is passive.
column29: Where is there more dissolved sugar: in the gummy bear or in the plain water?

column9: Fresh cucumbers soaked in a very salty brine become limp, shriveled pickles. What causes this?
column14: Salt enters the cucumber cells by active transport and makes them heavy
column15: The brine is hypotonic, so water enters the cucumber cells
column16: The brine is hypertonic, so water leaves the cucumber cells by osmosis
column17: The cucumber's cell walls dissolve in salt
column28: Brine has much more salt than the cucumber cells, so it is hypertonic. Water moves out of the cells by osmosis toward the salty side, and the cucumber goes limp. A common mistake is thinking salt rushing in causes the change; it is water leaving that matters.
column29: Water moves toward the side with more solute.

column9: Match each real example to the form of transport it shows.
column14: A steroid hormone (a small lipid) slipping through the membrane :: Simple diffusion
column15: Water moving into a carrot slice sitting in fresh water :: Osmosis
column16: A nerve cell releasing chemical messengers from vesicles :: Exocytosis
column17: A Paramecium taking in a food particle :: Endocytosis
column18: A kidney cell pumping glucose back in against its gradient :: Active transport
column28: Small lipids pass right through the lipid bilayer (simple diffusion). Water crossing a membrane is osmosis. Releasing from vesicles is exocytosis, taking in food is endocytosis, and moving against a gradient is active transport. Students often call the Paramecium example exocytosis; it is bringing food in.
column29: Key clues: lipid, water, vesicles out, food in, against its gradient.

column9: Cells in your thyroid gland keep pulling in iodide ions from the blood, even though there is already about 30 times more iodide inside the cells than in the blood. What form of transport is this?
column14: Simple diffusion
column15: Facilitated diffusion
column16: Osmosis
column17: Active transport
column28: With 30 times more iodide inside, moving more in means going from low to high concentration. That requires energy and a pump, so it is active transport. Facilitated diffusion could only move iodide from high to low.
column29: Is the iodide moving with its gradient or against it?

column9: Why does the sodium-potassium pump need ATP, while osmosis does not?
column14: The pump moves ions against their concentration gradient
column15: Ions are heavier than water
column16: Osmosis only happens in plants
column17: The pump moves ions from high to low concentration, like diffusion
column28: Moving ions from low to high concentration is against the gradient, which takes energy. Osmosis moves water down its gradient, so it is free. Weight has nothing to do with it, and osmosis happens in all cells.
column29: Which way does the pump move ions compared with their gradient?

column9: Facilitated diffusion and active transport both use membrane proteins. What is the key difference between them?
column14: Facilitated diffusion carries materials in vesicles, while active transport moves them only through proteins
column15: Active transport uses energy to move materials against the gradient; facilitated diffusion does not
column16: Facilitated diffusion only moves water
column17: There is no difference; they are two names for the same process that uses proteins
column28: Both use proteins, but active transport spends ATP to move low to high, while facilitated diffusion is passive and moves high to low. Neither uses vesicles. A common mistake is thinking any protein means active.
column29: Compare the energy cost and the direction.

column9: Oxygen can cross the cell membrane on its own, but glucose needs a protein. Why?
column14: Oxygen is a gas, and only gases are able to slip between the phospholipids
column15: Glucose is larger and polar, so the oily middle of the bilayer blocks it
column16: Glucose is always moving against its gradient, so it needs a pump
column17: Oxygen uses ATP to get through
column28: Oxygen is small and nonpolar, so it slips between the phospholipid tails. Glucose is bigger and polar, so it needs a carrier protein (facilitated diffusion). Water, a liquid, also crosses membranes, so being a gas is not the reason.
column29: Think about size and how the molecule gets along with the oily tails.

column9: Put these steps in order for how a cell makes a protein and ships it out of the cell.
column14: The Golgi apparatus packages the protein into a vesicle
column15: A ribosome on the rough ER builds the protein
column16: The vesicle fuses with the cell membrane and releases the protein (exocytosis)
column17: The vesicle travels to the cell membrane
column18: The protein moves through the ER to the Golgi apparatus
column28: Ribosome builds it → ER → Golgi packages it → vesicle travels → vesicle fuses and releases it by exocytosis. A common mistake is putting the Golgi before the ER; the Golgi is the last stop before shipping, like a post office.
column29: Think of a factory: build, move to shipping, package, deliver.

column9: Cyanide is a poison that stops cells from making ATP. In a cell poisoned with cyanide, which process would keep going?
column14: The sodium-potassium pump
column15: Exocytosis of hormones
column16: Osmosis
column17: A white blood cell engulfing bacteria
column28: Osmosis is passive, so it does not need ATP and continues. The pump, exocytosis, and engulfing (endocytosis) all need ATP, so they stop. Students sometimes pick the pump because it is a protein that is already in place, but it cannot run without ATP.
column29: Which choice is passive?

column9: A class measured how long a drop of dye took to spread evenly through beakers of water: 0 °C: 20 min, 20 °C: 10 min, 60 °C: 3 min. Predict the time at 40 °C.
column14: About 25 minutes
column15: About 15 minutes
column16: About 6 minutes
column17: About 1 minute
column28: The time drops as temperature rises, and 40 °C is between 20 °C (10 min) and 60 °C (3 min), so the answer must fall between 3 and 10 minutes. About 6 minutes is the only choice in that range. Warmer particles move faster, so diffusion speeds up.
column29: 40 °C is between two of the temperatures that were tested. Which times does that put it between?

column9: In which situation would oxygen diffuse into a cell the FASTEST?
column14: Outside: 10 units, inside: 9 units
column15: Outside: 20 units, inside: 2 units
column16: Outside: 5 units, inside: 5 units
column17: Outside: 8 units, inside: 12 units
column28: The bigger the difference (the steeper the gradient), the faster diffusion happens. 20 − 2 = 18 is the biggest difference into the cell. 5 and 5 is equilibrium (no net movement), and 8 outside vs. 12 inside would send oxygen out of the cell.
column29: Subtract inside from outside for each choice.

column9: A cell has 10 mM glucose inside and 4 mM glucose outside. Glucose carrier proteins in the membrane are open, and no ATP is used. What happens?
column14: Glucose moves into the cell by active transport using carriers
column15: Glucose moves into the cell by facilitated diffusion
column16: Glucose does not move, because a protein is involved and no ATP is used
column17: Glucose moves out of the cell by facilitated diffusion
column28: Glucose moves from high (10 mM inside) to low (4 mM outside), so it leaves the cell. It uses a carrier protein with no ATP, which is facilitated diffusion. A common mistake is assuming glucose always moves into cells.
column29: First decide which side is higher. Molecules move down their gradient on their own.

column9: Human red blood cells are about 0.9% salt inside. A drop of blood is mixed with a 5% salt solution and viewed under a microscope. How will the red blood cells look?
column14: Shriveled and spiky
column15: Swollen and round, some bursting
column16: Exactly normal
column17: Filled with salt crystals
column28: 5% salt is hypertonic to a 0.9% cell, so water leaves the cells by osmosis and they shrivel (they often look spiky). Swelling and bursting would happen in a hypotonic solution like distilled water.
column29: Compare 5% with 0.9%. Which way will water move?

column9: Select every statement that is true of BOTH endocytosis and exocytosis. Select all that apply.
column14: They use vesicles
column15: They require energy from the cell
column16: They can move large materials, such as proteins, that are too big to pass through the membrane on their own
column17: They move material only out of the cell
column18: They happen without changing the shape of the membrane
column28: Both kinds of bulk transport use vesicles, take energy, and move large materials like proteins. Only exocytosis sends material out, so that statement is not true of both. Both change the membrane's shape as vesicles pinch off or fuse with it.
column29: One brings things in and one sends things out. What do they share?

column9: People stranded at sea are warned not to drink seawater, because it makes their cells lose even more water. Why?
column14: Seawater is hypotonic to body cells, so water rushes into the cells
column15: Seawater is hypertonic to body cells, so water moves out by osmosis
column16: Salt in seawater blocks the sodium-potassium pump so cells can't hold water
column17: Seawater is isotonic, so nothing happens
column28: Seawater is much saltier than body fluids, so it makes the fluid around cells hypertonic. Water moves out of the cells toward the salt, which dehydrates them. A common mistake is thinking any water you drink must hydrate you.
column29: Seawater is saltier than the inside of your cells. Water moves toward more solute.

column9: Which pair is correctly matched?
column14: Facilitated diffusion: active, uses ATP
column15: Exocytosis: passive, no vesicle needed
column16: Osmosis: passive, movement of water across a membrane
column17: Sodium-potassium pump: passive, moves ions from high to low
column28: Osmosis is passive and is water crossing a membrane. Facilitated diffusion is passive (no ATP), exocytosis is active and uses vesicles, and the sodium-potassium pump is active and moves ions low to high.
column29: Check each half of every pair. Only one pair has both halves right.

column9: Each cycle of the sodium-potassium pump uses 1 ATP and moves 3 sodium ions out of the cell and 2 potassium ions in. How many sodium ions does the pump move out when it uses 40 ATP?
column28: 40 ATP × 3 sodium ions per ATP = 120 sodium ions. A common mistake is using the potassium number (2 × 40 = 80) or adding the ions together (5 × 40 = 200).
column29: Use only the sodium number for each ATP.

column9: An Elodea leaf has been sitting in salt water, and its cells are plasmolyzed. A student rinses it and places it in fresh water. What should she see under the microscope after a few minutes?
column14: The cells shrink even more
column15: The cell walls burst open
column16: Nothing changes, because once a cell is plasmolyzed the damage is always permanent
column17: The cells take in water and the membranes press back against the cell walls
column28: Fresh water is hypotonic to the cells, so water moves back in by osmosis and the membranes swell back out against the walls. Plant cell walls keep the cells from bursting. Plasmolysis can often be reversed if the cell is not left in salt too long.
column29: Fresh water has less solute than the cells. Which way does water go now?

column9: A plant cell placed in a hypertonic solution will burst because its cell wall cannot stretch.
column28: False. In a hypertonic solution, water LEAVES the plant cell, so it shrinks (plasmolysis); it does not burst. Plant cells also rarely burst in a hypotonic solution, because the wall pushes back. A common mistake is mixing up which solution makes water enter.
column29: Does water move into or out of a cell in a hypertonic solution?

column9: A goldfish lives in a freshwater pond. Its body fluids have more dissolved salt than the pond water. Which way does water tend to move across the fish's gills and skin?
column14: Into the fish's body, by osmosis
column15: Out of the fish's body, by osmosis
column16: It does not move at all
column17: Into the fish, by active transport
column28: The pond water is hypotonic to the fish's body, so water tends to move in by osmosis. That is why freshwater fish make lots of dilute urine to get rid of the extra water. The movement of water is passive, not active.
column29: Water moves toward the side with more solute. Which side is saltier?

column9: Which statement best describes how diffusion and osmosis are related?
column14: They are opposites
column15: Osmosis is a kind of diffusion: water moving across a selectively permeable membrane
column16: Diffusion uses energy from ATP, but osmosis does not, so they are different processes
column17: Osmosis only moves salt across a membrane, and diffusion only moves water through it
column28: Osmosis is diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane, so it is a type of diffusion. Both are passive; neither uses energy. A common mistake is thinking osmosis moves salt or sugar, but only the water moves in osmosis.
column29: Is osmosis a different process, or a specific case of one you already know?

column9: A dialysis bag filled with 20% sugar solution is weighed and placed in a beaker of distilled water. The bag lets water through but not sugar. What will happen to the bag's mass after one hour?
column14: It will decrease
column15: It will stay the same
column16: It will increase
column17: It will drop to zero
column28: The distilled water is hypotonic to the 20% sugar inside the bag, so water moves into the bag by osmosis and the mass goes up. The sugar can't leave, so it can't balance the concentrations that way.
column29: Which side has more solute? Water moves toward it.

column9: A drop of dye spreads quickly through water at first, but the spreading slows down as time goes on. Why does diffusion slow down?
column14: The dye particles get tired and slow down as they move
column15: The water starts using ATP
column16: The concentration gradient gets smaller as the dye spreads
column17: The dye particles get bigger as they soak up water, so they move slower
column28: Diffusion is fastest when the gradient is steepest. As the dye spreads, the difference between crowded and empty areas shrinks, so the net movement slows until equilibrium is reached. Particles don't get tired; they keep moving the whole time.
column29: Compare the difference in concentration at the start with the difference later.

column9: Select every example that uses a membrane protein to move the substance. Select all that apply.
column14: Oxygen slipping between the phospholipids of a lung cell
column15: Glucose entering a red blood cell through a carrier
column16: A nerve cell pumping sodium out using ATP
column17: A small lipid passing straight through the bilayer
column18: Potassium ions flowing through an open ion channel
column28: Carriers, pumps, and ion channels are all membrane proteins, so the glucose, sodium, and potassium examples use one. Oxygen and small lipids pass straight through the bilayer (simple diffusion). A common mistake is thinking a protein always means the cell is spending energy; the glucose and potassium examples are passive.
column29: Look for the words carrier, pump, or channel.

column9: Two different cells are placed in the same beaker of solution. Cell A swells and Cell B shrinks. What does this tell you?
column14: Both cells started with the same solute concentration
column15: Cell A had a higher solute concentration than the solution, and Cell B had a lower one
column16: Cell A had a lower solute concentration than the solution, and Cell B had a higher one
column17: The solution is isotonic to both cells
column28: Water moves toward more solute. Cell A gained water, so it had more solute than the solution (the solution was hypotonic to A). Cell B lost water, so it had less solute than the solution (hypertonic to B). The same solution can be hypotonic to one cell and hypertonic to another.
column29: For each cell, ask: did water move toward the cell or away from it?

column9: A dried raisin with a mass of 1.0 g soaks in water and its mass becomes 1.8 g. By what percent did its mass increase?
column28: Percent change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100 = (1.8 − 1.0) ÷ 1.0 × 100 = 80%. A common mistake is dividing by the final mass (0.8 ÷ 1.8 ≈ 44%). The raisin gained mass because water moved in by osmosis.
column29: Find the change in mass, then divide by the STARTING mass and multiply by 100.

column9: Which everyday situation is the best model of facilitated diffusion?
column14: Workers using a powered elevator to carry boxes up to a crowded top floor
column15: People spreading out across an open field with no walls
column16: A delivery truck dropping off packages at a store
column17: People leaving a packed gym through an open door into an empty hallway
column28: In facilitated diffusion, molecules move from crowded to less crowded (high to low) through a specific opening (a protein), with no energy. People leaving a packed gym through a door fits. The powered elevator models active transport, the open field models simple diffusion, and the truck is more like a vesicle.
column29: Look for crowded to empty, through a specific opening, with no power.

column9: Oxygen enters cells by simple diffusion, and glucose often enters by facilitated diffusion. What do these two processes have in common?
column14: Both use a carrier protein to get across the cell membrane
column15: Both move material down its gradient without using ATP
column16: Both use vesicles
column17: Both move material from low to high concentration, like a pump
column28: Both are passive: they move materials high to low and use no ATP. Only facilitated diffusion uses a protein, neither uses vesicles, and moving low to high would be active transport.
column29: Both are in the same group of transport. Which group?

column9: Root hair cells have many more mitochondria than most other plant cells. What does this suggest about root hair cells?
column14: They pump in minerals by active transport, which uses a lot of ATP
column15: They do photosynthesis all day long, so they need extra energy organelles
column16: They only use osmosis
column17: They never need energy
column28: Mitochondria make ATP. Cells with lots of mitochondria use lots of energy, and root hairs use it to pump in minerals that are scarce in the soil. Roots are underground, so they do not do much photosynthesis, and osmosis does not require ATP.
column29: Mitochondria make ATP. What kind of transport uses ATP?

column9: A membrane lets BOTH water and salt pass through. One side starts with salt water and the other with pure water. What happens over time?
column14: Only water moves, toward the salty side, until that side overflows
column15: Salt moves toward the pure water and water toward the salty side until the concentrations match
column16: Nothing moves, because a membrane that lets both substances through cannot have a gradient across it
column17: All the salt moves to the pure water side and stays there, leaving pure water behind
column28: Since salt can cross, it diffuses down its gradient into the pure water while water also moves toward the saltier side. They move until the concentrations match (equilibrium). Osmosis causes big volume changes only when the solute CAN'T cross.
column29: Both substances can cross. Each one moves down its own gradient.

column9: A membrane made of only phospholipids (no proteins) is tested. Put these from the one that crosses MOST easily to the one that crosses LEAST easily.
column14: Glucose (large, polar)
column15: Oxygen (small, nonpolar)
column16: Sodium ion, Na⁺ (charged)
column17: Water (small, polar)
column28: Small nonpolar oxygen slips through easily. Water is small, so a little gets through even though it is polar. Glucose is larger and polar, so it barely crosses. Charged ions like Na⁺ are almost completely blocked by the oily tails. A common mistake is ranking by size alone and putting the tiny Na⁺ ion first.
column29: Charge is the biggest barrier, then size and polarity.

column9: A dialysis bag is filled with iodine solution and placed in a beaker of starch water. Iodine molecules are small enough to pass through the bag, but starch molecules are not. Iodine turns blue-black when it touches starch. After 20 minutes, what will you see?
column14: The liquid inside the bag turns blue-black
column15: The water in the beaker turns blue-black
column16: Both the bag and the beaker turn blue-black
column17: Neither one changes color
column28: Iodine diffuses out of the bag into the beaker, where it meets starch, so the beaker turns blue-black. Starch is too large to get into the bag, so the inside stays the iodine color. A common mistake is assuming the color always shows up inside the bag.
column29: Figure out which molecule can travel, then where the two molecules can meet.

column9: A Paramecium from a freshwater pond is moved into water that is slightly saltier, but still less salty than the inside of the Paramecium. What will most likely happen to how often its contractile vacuole pumps out water?
column14: It pumps more often, because more water is rushing in
column15: It stops for good, because the water around it is now hypertonic
column16: It pumps less often, because less water is entering by osmosis
column17: It does not change at all
column28: The new water is still hypotonic, but closer to the cell's concentration, so the gradient is smaller and less water enters. The vacuole has less extra water to remove, so it pumps less often. It is not hypertonic, because it is still less salty than the cell.
column29: Did the difference in concentration between the cell and the water get bigger or smaller?

column9: A cube of carrot has a mass of 5.0 g. After an hour in a salt solution, its mass is 4.0 g. By what percent did its mass decrease? (Enter a positive number.)
column28: Percent change = (5.0 − 4.0) ÷ 5.0 × 100 = 20% decrease. Water left the carrot cells by osmosis, so the salt solution was hypertonic to the carrot. A common mistake is dividing by the final mass: 1.0 ÷ 4.0 = 25%.
column29: Divide the change by the STARTING mass.

column9: A cell is 98% water inside. It is placed in a solution that is 90% water. Assuming the solute cannot cross the membrane, which way will water move overall?
column14: Into the cell, because the solution has more solute to pull it
column15: It will not move, because both are mostly water
column16: Into the cell, because the cell starts out with more water in it
column17: Out of the cell, toward the solution, which has less water
column28: Water moves from where there is more water (98% in the cell) to where there is less water (90% in the solution). That means it leaves the cell, which is the same as saying the solution is hypertonic (more solute: 10% vs. 2%). A common mistake is thinking water moves toward the side with more water.
column29: Turn water percents into solute percents: 98% water means 2% solute.

column9: A cell's inside is 0.5% salt. It is placed in a 0.1% salt solution, and salt cannot cross the membrane. Select every statement that is true. Select all that apply.
column14: The solution is hypotonic to the cell
column15: Water will move into the cell overall
column16: The cell is hypertonic compared with the solution
column17: The cell will shrink
column18: The solution is hypertonic to the cell
column28: The solution (0.1%) has less solute than the cell (0.5%), so the solution is hypotonic, the cell is hypertonic compared with it, and water moves into the cell, so it swells rather than shrinks. A common mistake is forgetting that hypotonic and hypertonic always compare two things; the same pair can be described from either side.
column29: Describe it from both sides: the solution compared with the cell, and the cell compared with the solution.

column9: A U-shaped tube is split down the middle by a membrane that lets water through but not sucrose. Side A holds 10% sucrose solution and Side B holds 2% sucrose solution. Both start at the same height. After an hour, what will you see?
column14: The water level on Side A rises
column15: The water level on Side B rises
column16: Both sides stay level
column17: Sucrose moves from Side A to Side B
column28: Side A has more solute, so water moves from B to A by osmosis, raising the level on Side A. Sucrose can't cross, so it can't even out that way. A common mistake is predicting that the sucrose moves; in osmosis only the water crosses.
column29: Water moves toward the side with more solute. Which side is that?

column9: The cholera bacterium makes a toxin that causes cells lining the intestine to release large amounts of chloride and other salts into the intestine. People with cholera lose huge amounts of water as diarrhea. Which explanation best connects these facts?
column14: The salts make the intestine hypertonic, so water leaves body cells by osmosis into the intestine
column15: The salts make the intestine contents hypotonic, so water moves out of it into the intestine cells
column16: The bacteria pump water out of the body's cells by active transport into the intestine
column17: Water follows the salts by endocytosis
column28: Extra salts in the intestine raise its solute concentration, making it hypertonic to the cells around it. Water moves by osmosis toward the higher solute concentration, into the intestine, and leaves the body. This is why cholera treatment replaces both water and salts. Students often think the water itself is being pumped, but osmosis is passive.
column29: Where is the solute concentration now highest? Water follows solute.

column9: A student writes: "Osmosis is when salt moves across a membrane into the cell." Which correction is best?
column14: Osmosis is when salt moves out of the cell, toward the side with less solute
column15: Osmosis is water, not salt, moving across a membrane toward the side with more solute
column16: Osmosis is when the cell uses ATP to pump salt across a selectively permeable membrane
column17: The statement is correct
column28: In osmosis, the water moves, not the salt. Water moves across a selectively permeable membrane toward the side with more solute. Salt moving would be diffusion (or active transport if pumped). Mixing up the solute and the water is the most common osmosis mistake.
column29: In osmosis, which substance is actually crossing?

column9: A student wants to test whether temperature affects how fast dye diffuses in water. Which setup is a fair test?
column14: Use cold water in a small cup and hot water in a large bowl, with a different dye in each one
column15: Use the same amount of water and the same dye in each cup, and change only the temperature
column16: Stir the hot cup but not the cold cup
column17: Test only hot water, because it is faster
column28: In a fair test, only the variable being tested (temperature) changes; everything else (amount of water, dye, cup size, no stirring) stays the same. Stirring or using different cups would change the results for reasons other than temperature, and one temperature alone can't show an effect.
column29: Only one thing should be different between the cups.

column9: Cores of beet were soaked in sugar solutions for a day and their mass change was measured: 0.0 M: +12%, 0.2 M: +5%, 0.4 M: −3%, 0.6 M: −10%. The beet cells' own concentration is closest to which range?
column14: Between 0.0 and 0.2 M
column15: Between 0.2 and 0.4 M
column16: Between 0.4 and 0.6 M
column17: Higher than 0.6 M
column28: The isotonic point is where the mass change would be zero. Mass went up at 0.2 M (+5%) and down at 0.4 M (−3%), so zero change, and the cells' concentration, falls between 0.2 and 0.4 M. A common mistake is choosing the solution with the biggest change instead of looking for where the sign switches.
column29: Look for where the mass change switches from gaining to losing.

column9: Scientists measure how fast glucose enters a cell by facilitated diffusion. As the outside glucose concentration rises, the rate goes up at first, but then it levels off and stays flat even when much more glucose is added. What is the best explanation?
column14: The cell ran out of ATP
column15: Glucose started moving back out of the cell by active transport to balance it
column16: All the carrier proteins are busy, so more glucose can't speed it up
column17: The membrane became impermeable to water
column28: Facilitated diffusion depends on a limited number of carrier proteins. Once every carrier is working as fast as it can, extra glucose has to wait its turn, so the rate levels off. It does not use ATP, so running out of ATP is not the cause. Simple diffusion, which needs no protein, would keep speeding up.
column29: What is limited in facilitated diffusion that is not limited in simple diffusion?

column9: Nerve cells keep far more potassium inside than outside, even though potassium constantly leaks out through channels. How does the cell keep its potassium level high inside?
column14: Potassium moves back in by simple diffusion
column15: Potassium enters by osmosis
column16: The leaking stops on its own once potassium reaches equilibrium across the membrane
column17: The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to move potassium back in against its gradient
column28: Leaking out through channels is passive (facilitated diffusion). To keep the inside high, the cell must move potassium back in from low to high, which takes the sodium-potassium pump and ATP. Diffusion would only move potassium out, and osmosis is for water.
column29: Moving potassium back in means moving it which way compared with its gradient?

column9: A molecule enters a cell through a membrane protein. The concentration of this molecule is 2 mM outside and 8 mM inside. What form of transport is this?
column14: Active transport
column15: Facilitated diffusion
column16: Simple diffusion
column17: Osmosis
column28: It is moving from 2 mM (low) to 8 mM (high), which is against its gradient. That requires energy, so it is active transport, even though the protein might make you think of facilitated diffusion. A common mistake is classifying only by "uses a protein" without checking direction.
column29: Check the direction first: is it moving from high to low or low to high?

column9: Which changes would make oxygen diffuse into a cell FASTER? Select all that apply.
column14: Raising the temperature
column15: Increasing the oxygen concentration outside the cell
column16: Making the concentration gradient steeper
column17: Lowering the outside oxygen until it matches the inside
column28: Warmer particles move faster, and a steeper gradient (more oxygen outside compared with inside) speeds up diffusion. Matching the inside and outside removes the gradient, which stops net diffusion, and cooling slows particles down.
column29: Two things speed up diffusion: faster particles and a bigger difference in concentration.

column9: Match what a plant cell looks like to the type of solution it is sitting in.
column14: Cell is swollen and firm, pushing hard against its cell wall :: Hypotonic solution
column15: Membrane has shrunk and pulled away from the cell wall :: Hypertonic solution
column16: Cell is limp, but the membrane still touches the cell wall :: Isotonic solution
column28: In a hypotonic solution water enters and the cell gets firm (turgid), which is how plants like it. In a hypertonic solution water leaves and the membrane pulls away (plasmolysis). In an isotonic solution there is no net water movement, so the cell is limp but not plasmolyzed. Students often think isotonic is the best condition for plant cells; it is best for animal cells.
column29: Start with the one where water left the cell, then the one where water entered.

column9: A student says, "Once oxygen reaches equilibrium on both sides of a membrane, the oxygen molecules stop moving." How should you respond?
column14: Agree, because there is no gradient
column15: Disagree: molecules keep moving both ways, but equal numbers cross each way, so no net change
column16: Disagree: the molecules all move to one side and pile up there instead
column17: Agree, because the membrane closes at equilibrium and blocks any more molecules from getting across
column28: Particles never stop moving. At equilibrium, they keep crossing both ways at the same rate, so the concentrations stay equal. The net movement is zero, not the movement itself.
column29: Do particles ever stop their random motion?

column9: To make a salt solution for an osmosis lab, a student dissolves 10 g of salt in enough water to make 200 mL. What is the concentration in grams per 100 mL (percent)?
column28: 10 g ÷ 200 mL = 0.05 g per mL, and 0.05 × 100 = 5 g per 100 mL, or 5%. A common mistake is answering 20 by dividing 200 by 10.
column29: Find the grams in each mL first, then scale up to 100 mL.

column9: In the kidney, cells use ATP to pump sodium ions out of the tubule into the surrounding tissue. Water then follows the sodium out of the tubule. Which two forms of transport are happening, in order?
column14: Osmosis, then active transport
column15: Active transport, then osmosis
column16: Facilitated diffusion, then exocytosis
column17: Simple diffusion, then active transport
column28: Pumping sodium with ATP is active transport. That raises the solute concentration in the surrounding tissue, so water moves there by osmosis. A common mistake is thinking water is also pumped; cells move water by moving solutes and letting osmosis do the rest.
column29: Which step uses ATP? What does water do when solute builds up on one side?

column9: A cell's mass is measured every 10 minutes after it is put in a solution: 10.0 g, 9.4 g, 9.0 g, 8.8 g, 8.8 g. Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: The solution was hypotonic, so the cell kept gaining water until it leveled off
column15: The solution was isotonic the whole time
column16: The solution was hypertonic; the cell lost water until net movement stopped
column17: The cell used active transport to pump out water until it ran out of ATP
column28: The mass dropped, so water left the cell: the solution was hypertonic. The last two readings are the same, so net water movement stopped. A common mistake is reading the leveling off as a sign that the solution was isotonic from the start.
column29: First look at the direction of change, then at what happens at the end.

column9: A scientist wants evidence that a cell takes in a certain amino acid by active transport, not by diffusion. Which result would be the strongest evidence?
column14: The amino acid enters faster on warm days
column15: The amino acid enters through a membrane protein, and the protein changes shape as it works
column16: The amino acid keeps entering until the inside and outside concentrations are equal, then stops
column17: The inside level keeps rising above the outside level, and uptake stops when ATP is blocked
column28: Building up a higher concentration inside means moving against the gradient, and stopping when ATP is blocked shows the process needs energy. Both point to active transport. Using a protein alone could be facilitated diffusion, and stopping at equal concentrations is what diffusion does.
column29: Which result shows both moving against the gradient AND needing energy?

column9: Ocean fish constantly lose water to the salty sea, and they drink seawater to make up for it. Special cells in their gills then move extra salt out of the blood into the seawater, which is saltier than the blood. What form of transport do these gill cells use for the salt, and why?
column14: Active transport, because the salt moves from lower (blood) to higher concentration (seawater)
column15: Simple diffusion, because salt always moves out of cells
column16: Osmosis, because the fish is in water
column17: Facilitated diffusion, because the salt moves from high to low concentration through gill proteins
column28: The salt is moving into seawater that is saltier than the blood, which is against the gradient, so the gill cells must spend ATP: active transport. Osmosis only describes water. A common mistake is thinking salt naturally flows into the ocean because the ocean is salty; diffusion would actually move it the other way.
column29: Compare the salt concentration in the blood with the seawater. Which way is the salt going?

column9: Red blood cells are about 0.9% salt inside. Put these solutions in order from the one that would make the cells SWELL the most to the one that would make them SHRINK the most.
column14: 3% salt
column15: 0.45% salt
column16: Distilled water (0% salt)
column17: 0.9% salt
column28: Distilled water is the most hypotonic, so the most water rushes in. 0.45% is less hypotonic. 0.9% is isotonic (no change), and 3% is hypertonic, so water leaves and the cells shrink. A common mistake is ordering from most salt to least, which reverses the answer.
column29: The less salt in the solution compared with 0.9%, the more water enters.

column9: Cells use oxygen constantly in cellular respiration. Why does oxygen keep diffusing into a cell instead of reaching equilibrium and stopping?
column14: The cell pumps oxygen in using ATP
column15: The cell keeps using up oxygen, so the inside stays low and a gradient remains
column16: Oxygen can only move in one direction across a membrane, from outside to inside
column17: Oxygen enters by endocytosis
column28: Because the cell uses oxygen as fast as it arrives, the concentration inside stays low. That keeps a gradient between the outside (high) and the inside (low), so diffusion continues with no ATP needed. Membranes do not force one-way movement; the gradient decides the direction.
column29: What happens to the oxygen once it is inside the cell?

column9: The sodium-potassium pump keeps sodium ions much more concentrated outside a nerve cell than inside. When the nerve fires, sodium channels open. Which way do sodium ions move, and what form of transport is it?
column14: Out of the cell, by active transport
column15: Into the cell, by active transport
column16: Into the cell, by facilitated diffusion
column17: Out of the cell, by facilitated diffusion
column28: Sodium is higher outside, so when channels open it flows in, down its gradient. It goes through a channel protein without ATP, so it is facilitated diffusion. The pump that built the gradient was active, but the flow through the open channel is passive. Students often call it active because the pump is mentioned.
column29: First find where sodium is crowded. Then ask whether the channel itself needs energy.
